title: Tables, screens and what shows when
desc: Design an app's tables, add screens, build them from the component strip, and show a component only when it matters.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can design an app table by hand, tell it apart from a linked Studio table, add screens and build them from the component strip, choose the home screen and the menu, and show or enable a component only under a condition.

steps.title: Every app carries its own database
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep's purchase requests live in a shared spreadsheet that four people edit at the same time. In the previous chapter the AI built the screens for their **Inkoopaanvragen** app. The rows those screens show have to live somewhere, and that somewhere is the app's own database — private to this one app.

You open it from the editor header: switch the view control to **Data**. A dialog appears, titled **Tables** — *"Design the data behind your app, then drop a form or grid onto the current screen."* Its tabs are **Tables · Rows · Relationships · Connectors · People**.

The room is generous: up to 50 tables in an app, 100 fields in a table, 100 000 rows in a table and 256 MB of database in total.

steps.title: A field has a name, a column name and a type
steps.bodyMd:
Press **New table** and give it a **Table name**: `Aanvragen`. The hint underneath, *Stored as: aanvragen*, is the name the database itself uses.

Then **Add field** for each thing you want to keep. A field carries three things:

- **Name** — what people read on the screen.
- **Column name** — what the app refers to it by. It follows the name until you edit it yourself.
- **Type** — Text, Rich text, Number, Date, Date & time, Yes / no, Select, Multi-select, Relation, File or Computed.

Tick **Required** or **Unique** where it matters. A Select then asks for its **Choices**, a Relation for a **Related table**, a Computed field for an expression such as `price * quantity`.

Five names are taken before you start: every table already carries `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `created_by` and `org_id` — so never add a "who filled this in" field of your own.

steps.title: Pick the type for each thing Van Dijk stores
steps.instruction: Nadia listed what a purchase request has to record. Match each one to the field type you would choose in the designer.

pairs.left: The amount the site manager expects to spend, so the office can total the month
pairs.note: A Number can be compared, summed and charted; the same figure as Text cannot.

pairs.left: Whether the request is nieuw, goedgekeurd or afgewezen — always one of those three
pairs.note: A Select carries the choices you define, so nobody invents a fourth status by typing.

pairs.left: The day the materials have to be on site — the time of day is irrelevant
pairs.note: Date is a day with no time of day; Date & time is for a moment.

pairs.left: The supplier's quotation, as the PDF they e-mailed
pairs.note: A File field takes an attachment; 25 MB is the ceiling per file.

pairs.left: The line total the app works out from price and quantity — nobody types it
pairs.note: A Computed field is worked out from other fields, which is also why a form never offers an input for it.

steps.title: Saving is what actually builds the table
steps.bodyMd:
Until you press **Save changes**, your table exists only in the editor. Saving sends the model to the server, which compares it with what is already there and runs the difference: tables created, columns added, renamed or dropped.

The **Rows** tab stays disabled until that has happened — hover it and it says *"Save the table first — until then there is nowhere to keep its rows."*

A saved **Column name** then freezes: the editor shows it as *"Fixed — the app already refers to this field by this name."* A **Change…** button still forces it through, and the warning is honest about the price — every form, list and chart pointing at that field stops finding it.

Pick the type with the same care: changing a saved field's type rewrites nothing already stored, and the AI builder refuses such a conversion outright. Add a new field and move the values across.

steps.question: You have typed six fields into the new Aanvragen table, but the Rows tab is greyed out and its tooltip says "Save the table first — until then there is nowhere to keep its rows." What is going on?

choices.label: The table only exists in the editor so far. Press Save changes, the database is brought up to date, and the Rows tab opens.
The Rows tab only works for tables the AI builder created, not for ones you typed by hand.
choices.feedback: Rows makes no distinction. A table the AI made and a table you typed are the same kind of table — both are only real once the model has been saved.

choices.label: You have to publish the app before it can hold any rows.
choices.feedback: Publishing decides who may open the app and freezes a copy of the screens. Rows are data, not part of that copy — you can fill a table long before anyone else may see the app.

choices.label: The screen has no grid on it yet, so there is nowhere to show the rows.
choices.feedback: Rows is the editor's own row browser and needs no component on the canvas. What is missing is the table in the database, not a place to display it.

steps.explanation: The Data view edits a model; Save changes is what turns that model into real storage. Everything that touches rows — the Rows tab, the form generator — waits for that save.

steps.title: The second kind of table: linked
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep already keeps its suppliers in **Studio → Datatables**. Copying that list into the app would leave the office with two lists to maintain, so the app **links** it instead.

A linked table wears a **Linked** badge and the line **Linked to a Studio table** — *"The columns below describe what this app expects to find there. Changing them does not change the Studio table."* Beside it sits the mode: **Read only** or **Read and write**.

Its rows are read live and the app gets no storage of its own for it, so the **Rows** tab sends you elsewhere with the hint *"Rows come from a Studio table."*

A link hands out no access either. What a colleague sees through it is the strictest of three answers: their own access to that Studio table, the app owner's access to it, and what their role in the app allows.

steps.question: The app's Leveranciers table is linked to a Studio datatable. In the app's Data view you rename its field's column name from contact to contactpersoon and save. What have you changed?

choices.label: Only what this app expects to find in the Studio table — which now no longer matches, so the app looks for a column the source has not got.
The column in the Studio datatable is renamed too, and everything reading that table follows along.
choices.feedback: The strip above the fields says it outright: changing these columns does not change the Studio table. The app-side list only describes what the app expects to find there.

choices.label: Nothing — a linked table is read-only, so the editor refuses the rename.
choices.feedback: Read only and Read and write describe what the app may do to the rows, not whether you can edit the app-side column list. The rename is accepted; it is the result that hurts.

choices.label: The app copies the rows into its own database under the new column name.
choices.feedback: A linked table never gets storage inside the app — that is the whole point of linking. There is no copy for a rename to land in.

steps.explanation: An app-side column list on a linked table is an expectation, not a definition. Change the real column in Studio → Datatables, then ask the builder to refresh the link so the app's copy of the column names matches again.

steps.title: Make a form, make a grid
steps.bodyMd:
Under the field designer sits a panel called **Add to this screen**. While the table is unsaved it only says *"Save this table first, then you can drop a form or a list onto the screen."* and offers **Save now**. Once saved, two buttons appear.

**Make a form** drops a form onto the screen you are on, with one input per writable field: a Select becomes a dropdown carrying your choices, a File becomes an upload, a Computed field is skipped because nobody types it. Its submit button reads *Add Aanvragen*, and it arrives already wired — submitting creates the row and confirms it.

**Make a grid** drops a searchable grid bound to the same table's rows, one column per field.

On a **Read only** link you get only the grid: *"This link is read only, so there is no form to make — a grid can still show the rows."*

steps.title: Screens, and the strip you build them from
steps.bodyMd:
The tabs along the top of the canvas are the app's **screens**. **Add screen** makes another — it arrives as **Screen {n}** — and each tab's **Screen options** menu holds **Rename**, **Set as home screen**, **Delete screen** and **Manage navigation…**. Deleting is refused on the last one: *"An app needs at least one screen"*. Room for 40 screens in an app, 40 sections in a screen.

Everything else on a screen comes from the **Components** strip beside the canvas. Its first tab, **Start here**, is a shortcut to the eight you reach for most: heading, text, button, image, card, table, form and chart. **All** shows the complete set, split into **Basics · Content · Layout · Data · Input · AI**. There is a **Search a component…** box, and every card repeats the two ways in: *"Click to add — or drag it onto the canvas"*. **Hide the component strip** gives the canvas its room back.

So a form reaches a screen by either route — generated from the Data view already bound to a table, or dragged out of **Input** and wired by you.

steps.question: Nadia is standing on the Overzicht screen and wants a searchable list of the rows in the app's Aanvragen table, already bound to it, without wiring anything by hand. What does she do?

choices.label: Switch the header to Data, pick the Aanvragen table and press Make a grid under Add to this screen — it lands on the screen she is standing on, bound to that table.
Drag a Table out of the component strip's Data category; a table component finds the app's rows by itself.
choices.feedback: A component dragged from the strip arrives empty — you still point it at a table yourself. The generator is the route that arrives already bound.

choices.label: Press Add screen first — a grid can only be generated onto a fresh, empty screen.
choices.feedback: The generators drop onto the screen you are on, empty or not. Add screen simply makes one more page.

choices.label: Open Manage navigation… and add the table to the app's menu.
choices.feedback: Manage navigation groups screens into sections of the app's menu. It never puts data on a screen.

steps.explanation: Two routes onto the same canvas: the component strip (Basics · Content · Layout · Data · Input · AI) for anything you wire yourself, and the Data view's Make a form / Make a grid for something that arrives already bound to a table.

steps.title: Your turn: design the Inkoopaanvragen table
steps.instruction: Write the data model for Van Dijk Groep's purchase requests as a short list. For each field give a name, the type you would pick from the designer, and whether it is required. Cover at least: who is asking, the project, the supplier, what is being bought, the amount, the day it is needed, the status, and the supplier's quotation. Then add two sentences: which of these you would NOT store in the app's own table because it already exists in Studio → Datatables, and which field you deliberately did not create because every table already has it.
steps.placeholder: e.g. Aanvrager — Text, required · Project — Text, required · Leverancier — ... (then: the supplier list is already a Studio datatable, so I would link it rather than retype it; and I add no "submitted by" field because created_by ...)

steps.title: Put the build in order
steps.instruction: Nadia wants to add the table, check by hand that rows really land in it, and only then put a form on the screen. Put her five moves in the order that actually works.

items.label: In the editor, switch the header to Data and add the table and its fields on the Tables tab
Press Save changes so the table is really made
Open the Rows tab and type two test rows by hand
Under Add to this screen, press Make a form
Open Preview, submit the form and find the new row back under Rows

sim.feedback: Everything downstream of the model waits for the save: Rows stays disabled until then, and the generator builds the form from what was actually saved. Typing a couple of rows first means the grid has something to show and the preview submit is a change you can see.

steps.question: On the linked Leveranciers table, set to Read only, the Add to this screen panel offers Make a grid but no Make a form. Why is the form button missing?

choices.label: A form writes rows, and this link may only read — offering it would break at the first submission instead of at the moment you ask for it.
The generator only builds forms for tables with a handful of fields; a supplier list has too many.
choices.feedback: Field count has nothing to do with it. A form is generated with one input per writable field, however many there are.

choices.label: Forms can only be generated for tables the app created itself, never for linked ones.
choices.feedback: A link set to Read and write does get the form button. It is the mode that decides, not the fact that the table is linked.

choices.label: The app has not been published yet, and generators are disabled in a draft.
choices.feedback: The generators work in the draft — that is the only place you ever build. Publishing is about who may open the finished app.

steps.explanation: A Read only link says the app may look at those rows and nothing more. Refusing the form up front is kinder than a form that submits into a wall; the grid still shows the list.

steps.title: The home screen, and the menu people see
steps.bodyMd:
One screen is the **home screen**: the one the app opens on, marked with a little home badge on its tab. **Screen options → Set as home screen** moves it, and if you delete the home screen the badge falls to the first remaining screen.

**Screen options → Manage navigation…** opens **Manage navigation** — *"Group screens into sections. Grouped screens appear under their section in the sidebar; the tab bar shows them after the ungrouped ones."* Give a group a **Group label** (up to 40 characters) and an **Icon**, then tick the screens that belong to it. A screen can sit in one group only — tick it elsewhere and the dialog tells you which group already has it — and an app holds at most 10 groups.

Each screen also carries its own menu entry: an icon, a **Menu description** and a **Show in navigation** toggle. Turn that off for a screen you want reachable from a button but not from the menu.

steps.question: Van Dijk's app has an Overzicht screen and a Nieuwe aanvraag screen. The office should land on Overzicht, and Nieuwe aanvraag should be reachable only from the "Nieuwe aanvraag" button. Which pair of settings does that?

choices.label: Set as home screen on Overzicht, and Show in navigation off for Nieuwe aanvraag — the button still takes people there.
Set as home screen on Overzicht, and Delete screen on Nieuwe aanvraag — the button brings it back when it is clicked.
choices.feedback: Delete screen removes the screen and everything on it, and nothing recreates it. The button is then left pointing at an action that no longer exists — one of the things the editor flags on the canvas.

choices.label: Put both screens in one navigation group; the first screen of a group is the one the app opens on.
choices.feedback: Groups only decide how the menu is arranged — grouped screens under their section, ungrouped ones first in the tab bar. Which screen opens is Set as home screen and nothing else.

choices.label: Set as home screen on Overzicht, and hide Nieuwe aanvraag for everyone under Roles → Screen access.
choices.feedback: Screen access puts a screen out of reach for a role altogether, so the button would lead those people nowhere either. Show in navigation only keeps the screen out of the menu.

steps.explanation: Three separate questions, three separate controls: Set as home screen decides where people land, Show in navigation decides whether a screen appears in the menu, and Roles → Screen access decides who may open it at all.

steps.title: Show a component only when it matters
steps.bodyMd:
Select a component on the canvas and open the inspector's **Behaviour** tab. Under **Logic** sit three controls:

- **Visible** — a plain toggle: *"Hide this component from the running app."*
- **Only show when** — a formula, for example `form.priority == 'high'`. The component appears only while that comes out true.
- **Enabled when** — the same idea for usable rather than visible, for example `form.agree == true` on a submit button.

Empty the formula and the rule is gone again.

The canvas repeats every rule back at you as a badge on the node: **Hidden in the running app**, **Only shown when {expr}**, **Only usable when {expr}**. A component that has vanished in Preview is therefore never a mystery — its badge says so in Edit.

This is how a long form stays short: an *Andere leverancier* text box that only appears when the Select says so, a *Reden van afwijzing* box that waits for the status `afgewezen`.

steps.title: Which control hides which thing
steps.instruction: Four things Nadia wants out of the way in the Inkoopaanvragen app. Match each to the control that actually does it.

pairs.left: The submit button must stay greyed out until the requester ticks the "akkoord" box
pairs.note: Enabled when leaves the button in sight but unusable — the learner can see what is still missing.

pairs.left: An extra text box that should turn up only when the status is set to afgewezen
pairs.note: A formula such as form.status == 'afgewezen'; empty the field and the box is simply always there.

pairs.left: A heading you want to keep on the canvas for later, but nobody should see in the running app
pairs.note: The toggle reads "Hide this component from the running app", and the node wears the badge Hidden in the running app.

pairs.left: A screen that must stay out of the app's menu, yet still open when a button sends people to it
pairs.note: That is a screen setting, not a component one — and it is not the same as hiding the screen from a role under Roles → Screen access.

steps.title: Build it — we will verify it
steps.instruction: Open one of your own apps, or create one, and switch the header view control to Data. Add a table for the purchase requests with at least an aanvrager (Text), a bedrag (Number), a nodig op (Date) and a status (Select with nieuw, goedgekeurd, afgewezen). Press Save changes, open Rows and add one row by hand. Then press Add screen, use Make a form to put a working form on it, and set the other screen as the home screen. Finish by giving one component an Only show when rule and checking its badge on the canvas.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Design a table by hand.** Name, column name and type per field, Required and Unique where they matter, and **Save changes** to make it real — after which the column name is shown as fixed and changing the type rewrites nothing that is already stored.
- **Tell the two kinds of table apart.** The app's own storage, versus a **Linked** table whose rows stay in Studio → Datatables and whose access is the strictest of viewer, owner and app role.
- **Put data on a screen in one click.** **Make a form** for a wired form that creates rows, **Make a grid** for a searchable list — and you know why a Read only link offers only the second.
- **Build the screens themselves.** **Add screen**, the **Components** strip (**Start here** or **Basics · Content · Layout · Data · Input · AI**), **Set as home screen** and **Manage navigation…** for the menu people meet.
- **Show things only when they matter.** **Visible**, **Only show when** and **Enabled when** under the inspector's **Logic**, each repeated back as a badge on the node.

Next chapter: making the buttons do real work, so a submitted request does more than sit in a table.

ex-apps-data-and-screens-model.title: A workable purchase-request model
ex-apps-data-and-screens-model.task: The learner had to list the fields of an Inkoopaanvragen table with a name, a type from the designer's picker and whether it is required, then name one thing they would link from Studio → Datatables instead of storing, and one field they deliberately did not create because every table already has it.
criteria: Lists at least six fields, each with a type taken from the real picker (Text, Rich text, Number, Date, Date & time, Yes / no, Select, Multi-select, Relation, File, Computed) and a stated required / not required.
Picks defensible types rather than Text for everything: the amount is a Number, the date needed is a Date, the status is a Select (with its options named or implied), the quotation is a File.
Names the supplier list (or a comparable existing organisation list) as the thing to link to a Studio datatable rather than retype into the app.
Names at least one system column — id, created_at, updated_at, created_by or org_id — as the reason not to add a field of their own for it.
ex-apps-data-and-screens-model.guidance: Do not pass an answer that types everything as Text, that invents field types the picker does not offer, or that adds its own 'submitted by' / 'created on' field without noticing created_by and created_at. An answer that lists fields well but says nothing about linking or about system columns is incomplete — both of those sentences were asked for. Dutch or English field names are equally fine, and extra sensible fields are a plus, not a fault.

practiceTopic.title: An app's tables and screens
practiceTopic.summary: How an app's own tables, fields and linked Studio datatables are designed and saved, and how screens, the component strip and visibility rules put them in front of people.
facts: The editor's Data view opens a dialog titled Tables with the tabs Tables, Rows, Relationships, Connectors and People, where the field type picker offers Text, Rich text, Number, Date, Date & time, Yes / no, Select, Multi-select, Relation, File and Computed.
Every app table already carries id, created_at, updated_at, created_by and org_id, so a field of your own can never use one of those names.

Save changes is what brings the database up to date; until it has run, the Rows tab is disabled with the tooltip 'Save the table first — until then there is nowhere to keep its rows.' A saved field's column name is then shown as fixed and needs a Change… button to rename.
A linked table shows a Linked badge, a Read only or Read and write mode, and keeps its rows in a Studio datatable; the app gets no storage of its own for it.
Under Add to this screen, Make a form drops a form with one input per writable field that creates a row on submit, and Make a grid drops a searchable grid bound to the table's rows.

Screen tabs carry Add screen and a Screen options menu with Rename, Set as home screen, Delete screen and Manage navigation…; the last screen cannot be deleted ('An app needs at least one screen'), and the home screen is the one the app opens on.
The Components strip has a Start here tab and the categories Basics, Content, Layout, Data, Input and AI, a 'Search a component…' box and the card tip 'Click to add — or drag it onto the canvas'.

A component's Logic block holds Visible ('Hide this component from the running app'), Only show when and Enabled when — formulas whose effect the canvas repeats as the badges Hidden in the running app, Only shown when {expr} and Only usable when {expr}.

actionChecks.label: Design a table in one of your apps
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Apps, open an app you own, switch the header to Data, add a table with a few fields and press Save changes.

endpoints.returns: { apps: [ { id, userId, name, … } ] } — only the apps the signed-in learner owns

criteria.label: You own at least one app
criteria.hint: Studio → Apps → New app, or open one you built in the previous chapter.

criteria.label: That table has fields of your own
criteria.hint: Add at least two fields beside the columns every table already carries.
criteria.rule: that same table row has fields.length >= 2
